Dice 3 and 1 are revealed, so the known part of the sum is 5 + 2 = 7. Die 2 is still hidden and is 1, 2, 11 or 11. The settlement value is therefore 8 or 9 (each 1/4) or 18 (1/2), giving a fair value of 13.25.

The earlier trades tell us nothing more about die 2. Both sales to me were at prices below 8, the lowest value now possible, so they came from noise traders, not informed ones. The quotes with no trade are also consistent with every remaining value.

**Ask side:** At an ask of 18 or higher, an informed trader never buys. Only noise traders buy, and each sale earns me the gap above 13.25. That expected profit peaks at about 0.83 with an ask of roughly 20 to 21, so I quote 20.5.

**Bid side:** At a bid of 8 or lower, an informed trader never sells. Again only noise traders trade. The expected profit peaks at about 0.83 with a bid of roughly 6 to 7, so I quote 6.5. A bid just under 9 would buy from informed traders holding an 8, and that drops the expected profit to about 0.6.

I am long 2, so either fill keeps me inside the position limits.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 20.5}

Die 3 = 5 and die 1 = 2 are known, so the settlement is 7 plus die 2.

- **Possible values:** die 2 is one of {1, 2, 11, 11}, so the settlement is 8, 9, 18 or 18.
- **What the last trade tells us:** someone sold at 6.5 in quote 7. An informed trader would never sell that low, since every possible value is at least 8. So that seller was a noise trader, and the trade says nothing about die 2.
- **Fair value:** the probabilities stay ¼ for 8, ¼ for 9 and ½ for 18. That gives a fair value of 13.25.

**Ask side:**
- Any ask below 18 gets bought by informed traders whenever the value is 18, which loses money.
- At 18 or above, only noise traders buy. Noise traders value the contract at 13.25 plus normal noise with SD 9.8.
- My expected gain per quote is roughly the distance from 13.25 times the chance a noise trader trades there.
- For normal noise, that gain is largest about 0.75 SDs from the mean. That is about 7.35 above 13.25, so the ask is about 20.6.

**Bid side:**
- Any bid at or below 8 is never hit by informed traders, so only noise traders sell.
- The same calculation puts the best bid about 7.35 below 13.25, at about 5.9.

Being long 3 doesn't change expected profit. Filling the bid would take me to +4 and block my bid on the last quote, which costs very little.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 20.6}

With dice 1 and 3 revealed (2 + 5 = 7), settlement is 7 + die 2, so it can only be 8, 9 or 18.

**Updating the odds of die 2 from the trade history**

Only one trade carries information about die 2: quote 1, where someone sold to me at 9.4.
- An informed trader would sell there if the value were 8 or 9.
- An informed trader would not sell if the value were 18.
- A noise trader sells at 9.4 with probability Φ((9.4 − 18.92)/9.8) ≈ 0.17, where 18.92 was the starting fair value.

| Die 2 | Settlement | Prior | Chance of a sale at 9.4 | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 | 0.25 | 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.17 = 0.583 | ≈ 0.4375 |
| 2 | 9 | 0.25 | 0.583 | ≈ 0.4375 |
| 11 | 18 | 0.5 | 0.5 × 0.17 = 0.083 | ≈ 0.125 |

The other quotes tell us nothing new:
- Quotes 2–6 had the same outcome whichever of 8, 9 or 18 was true.
- The stage 3 trades (a sale at 6.5 and a purchase at 20.6) must both have been noise traders, since an informed trader would do neither.

The fair value is 8 × 0.4375 + 9 × 0.4375 + 18 × 0.125 ≈ 9.69.

**Choosing the ask**
- At an ask of 18.0, an informed trader never buys, because the value is at most 18.
- A noise trader buys with probability about 0.20 and pays about 8.3 above fair value.
- That gives an expected gain of about 0.5 × 0.198 × 8.31 ≈ 0.82.
- This is near the best ask, since lower asks lose to informed buyers when the value is 18.

**Choosing the bid**
- Any bid at or below 8 is never hit by an informed trader.
- Against noise traders alone, the gain (9.69 − b) × Φ((b − 9.69)/9.8) peaks at a bid of about 2.
- That gives an expected gain of about 0.5 × 0.216 × 7.69 ≈ 0.83.
- Buying one more unit takes my position to +3, which is within the +4 limit.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 18.0}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 15 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 0, 2 cards worth 4, 3 cards worth 9, 1 card worth 12, 3 cards worth 14, 2 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The fair value is about 23.8, and the spread needs to be wide, roughly ±11.

**Fair value**
- The deck totals 119 over 15 cards, so the mean card is 7.93.
- Expected sum of 3 cards: 3 × 7.93 ≈ 23.8.

**Uncertainty**
- Variance per card: E[x²] = 1457/15 ≈ 97.1, minus 7.93² ≈ 62.9, gives about 34.2.
- For 3 cards drawn without replacement: 3 × 34.2 × 12/14 ≈ 87.9.
- The settlement value's standard deviation is therefore about 9.4.

**Spread choice**
Informed traders know a value with a standard deviation of about 9.4. Noise traders are only off by about 7. Treating the settlement value as roughly normal:

| Half-width | Edge from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | +1.19 | −1.77 | Clear loss |
| 10 | +0.76 | −0.70 | About break-even |
| 11 | +0.64 | −0.56 | Small gain |

So I quote about ±11 around 23.8.

{"bid": 13.0, "ask": 35.0}

Fair value is about 23.8, and I'm quoting 13.8 / 34, about 10 either side of fair.

**Fair value.**
- The deck's values add to 0×4 + 4×2 + 9×3 + 12 + 14×3 + 15×2 = 119, so the average card is 119 / 15 ≈ 7.93.
- Three cards give an expected sum of about 23.8.
- The standard deviation of the 3-card sum, dealt without replacement, is about 9.4.

**Spread.**
- Half the counterparties know the exact value, and its spread (about 9.4) is larger than the noise traders' spread (7).
- So adverse selection is heavy, and a tight quote loses money on average.
- Using a normal approximation, a quote 6 either side of fair has negative expected profit.
- Quoting about 10 to 12 either side of fair is roughly break-even to slightly positive.
- The previous quote at 13 / 35 drew no trade, which tells us little.
- I keep the quote wide and centred near 23.8.

{"bid": 13.8, "ask": 34}

With card 1 revealed as 0, the settlement value is the sum of two more cards drawn from the 14 left.

**The value distribution**
- The 14 remaining cards add up to 119, so each card is worth 8.5 on average.
- The expected value of two cards is 17, which is the public fair value.
- I listed all 91 possible pairs to get the exact distribution of the sum.

**How I chose the quotes**
For each candidate price I weighed two things:
- **Noise traders (half the time):** they value the contract at 17 plus noise with standard deviation 7. A trade with them earns the gap between my price and 17, weighted by how likely they are to trade.
- **Informed traders (half the time):** they trade only when my price is wrong. A trade with them loses the gap between my price and the true sum, averaged over the 91 pairs.

**Ask side**
Expected profit per quote:

| Ask | 22 | 24 | 26 | 27 | 28 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expected profit | −0.02 | 0.23 | 0.28 | 0.28 | 0.28 |

The curve is flat around 26–28, and I picked 27.

**Bid side**
Expected profit per quote:

| Bid | 12 | 11 | 10 | 9 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Expected profit | −0.04 | 0.06 | 0.13 | 0.19 | 0.18 |

The best bid is about 9. At exactly 9, an informed trader whose sum is 9 values the contract at my bid and does not sell.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 27}

With card 1 = 0 revealed, I'd quote **bid 8.8, ask 26.5**. That is roughly the spread that maximises expected profit on each side.

**Fair value.** The 14 cards left sum to 119, so each averages 8.5. The expected settlement is 0 + 2 × 8.5 = 17. The no-trade at quote 3 doesn't move this, because a symmetric quote that nobody hits says little about direction.

**Settlement distribution.** The settlement is the sum of the two remaining cards. Out of 91 equally likely pairs, it ranges from 0 to 30, with a standard deviation of about 7.7.

**Choosing each side.** The expected edge on a side is half the noise trader's gain minus half the informed trader's loss:
- **Gain from noise traders:** the chance a noise trader (fair value 17, standard deviation 7) trades, times my edge over 17.
- **Loss to informed traders:** the expected amount by which the true settlement falls outside my quote.

**Ask side:**

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net, ×0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 24 | 1.11 | 0.66 | 0.22 |
| 26 | 0.89 | 0.33 | 0.28 |
| 27 | 0.77 | 0.20 | 0.28 |
| 28 | 0.64 | 0.09 | 0.27 |

The ask is best around 26–27.

**Bid side:**

| Bid | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net, ×0.5 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 0.77 | 0.43 | 0.17 |
| 8 | 0.89 | 0.53 | 0.18 |
| 9 | 1.01 | 0.64 | 0.18 |
| 10 | 1.11 | 0.85 | 0.13 |

The bid is best around 8–9.

{"bid": 8.8, "ask": 26.5}

Three cards are left unknown in total, but only card 3 remains hidden. The 13 cards still in the deck are:
- 0 ×3
- 4 ×2
- 9 ×3
- 12 ×1
- 14 ×2
- 15 ×2

These add up to 105, so the expected value of card 3 is 105/13 ≈ 8.08. Adding the revealed 0 and 14, the fair value is about **22.08**.

The possible settlement values are 14, 18, 23, 26, 28 and 29.

**Ask side.** A trader only buys if its valuation is strictly above my ask.
- At an ask of 29, no informed trader ever buys, because the maximum settlement is 29.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(N(22.08, 7) > 29) ≈ 0.16, and I earn about 6.9 when it does.
- Expected profit is about 0.56, the best of the asks I checked (28 gives about 0.51, 30 about 0.51).

**Bid side.** A trader only sells if its valuation is strictly below my bid.
- At a bid of 14, no informed trader ever sells, because the minimum settlement is 14.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 0.12, and I earn about 8.1 when it does.
- Expected profit is about 0.50, beating a bid of 15 (about 0.44) and a bid of 13 (about 0.44).

{"bid": 14, "ask": 29}

Answer: bid 14, ask 29. Both prices sit at the edges of the possible settlement values, so an informed trader never trades with me and the edge comes from noise traders.

**Settlement distribution.** The cards left after removing one 0 and one 14 are 0×3, 4×2, 9×3, 12×1, 14×2 and 15×2, which is 13 cards. Settlement is 14 plus card 3, so it is:
- 14 with probability 3/13
- 18 with probability 2/13
- 23 with probability 3/13
- 26 with probability 1/13
- 28 with probability 2/13
- 29 with probability 2/13

The expected value is about 22.08.

**The fill at quote 5 was a noise trader.** Settlement can't be below 14, so an informed trader would never have sold to me at 14. The public fair value therefore stays at about 22.08.

**Choosing the quote.** With one quote left, I compared expected profit across prices. A noise trader's valuation is roughly Normal with mean 22.08 and standard deviation 7.
- **Bid:**
  - At 14, an informed trader never sells, since they sell only if the value is strictly below the bid. Expected profit is about 0.50.
  - Raising the bid to 15 or 16 lets informed traders sell when the value is 14. That cuts expected profit to about 0.44 and 0.35.
- **Ask:**
  - At 29, an informed trader never buys, since they buy only if the value is strictly above the ask. Expected profit is about 0.56.
  - At 28, informed traders buy when the value is 29, which lowers expected profit to about 0.51.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 29}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 16 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 1 card worth 5, 3 cards worth 6, 1 card worth 7, 4 cards worth 8, 2 cards worth 9, 1 card worth 11, 3 cards worth 13. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
I'm quoting a bid of 11.5 and an ask of 21.5, centred on the expected sum of 16.5 with a half-spread of about 5.

**Fair value.** The 16 cards sum to 132, so the average card is 8.25. The expected sum of two cards is 16.5.

**Uncertainty.** A single card has a variance of about 8.94. For two cards drawn without replacement, the variance is 2 × 8.94 × 14/15 ≈ 16.7. That gives a standard deviation of about 4.1, close to the noise traders' spread.

**Spread.** I approximated both trader types as normal around 16.5 with standard deviation 4.1 and measured the half-spread as k standard deviations. Each side's expected profit is then roughly 0.5 × σ × [2k(1−Φ(k)) − φ(k)]:
- At k = 0.8 the bracket is about 0.049.
- At k = 1.0 it is about 0.075.
- At k = 1.2 it is about 0.082.
- At k = 1.4 it is about 0.077.

The best value is around k ≈ 1.2–1.25, a half-spread of about 5. This is only a normal approximation; the real distribution of the sum is discrete.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 21.5}

A buy at 21.5 points toward a high sum, so I raise fair value to about 19.8 and quote bid 15.0, ask 23.5.

**Prior.** The 16 cards sum to 132, so the average card is 8.25. The expected two-card sum is 16.5.

**What the buy at 21.5 tells me.**
- An informed trader buys only if the sum is 22 or more. Those pairs are 13+13 (3 pairs), 13+11 (3 pairs) and 13+9 (6 pairs). That is 12 of the 120 possible pairs, with an average sum of 23.5.
- A noise trader buys at 21.5 with probability about 0.11 whatever the sum is.
- After the buy, the high pairs get weight 0.555 each and all other pairs get 0.055 each. That puts about 53% probability on a high sum (average 23.5) and 47% on the rest (average about 15.7).
- The updated fair value is about **19.8**.

**Choosing the ask.**

| Ask | Informed buys when | Expected loss to informed | Expected gain from noise | Net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 21.5 | sum is 22+ | 0.53 | 0.31 | Negative |
| 22.5 | sum is 24+ | 0.33 | 0.34 | About zero |
| 23.5 | sum is 24+ | 0.20 | 0.34 | Positive |

An ask of about 23.5 is best.

**Choosing the bid.** At a bid near 15, an informed trader sells only when the sum is in the low part of the low group. That costs about 0.24, against about 0.32 expected from noise traders selling to me. A bid of 15 still comes out positive.

{"bid": 15.0, "ask": 23.5}

Posterior after the two buys: P(sum ∈ {24, 26}) ≈ 0.70, P(sum = 22) ≈ 0.11, P(sum ≤ 21) ≈ 0.19. The public fair value is about 22.9.

**How I got there**
- The 16-card deck gives 120 possible pairs, and the prior expected sum is 16.5.
- At quote 1 (ask 21.5), a noise trader buys about 11% of the time. An informed trader buys only if the sum is 22, 24 or 26 (12 of 120 pairs). This lifts the fair value to about 19.8.
- At quote 2 (ask 23.5), a noise trader buys about 18.5% of the time. An informed trader buys only if the sum is 24 or 26. This gives the posterior above.

**Ask:** At 26.1, no informed trader ever buys, because the highest possible sum is 26. Noise traders still lift it about 11% of the time, for about +3.2 each, so roughly +0.35 per quote. An ask near 25 would earn less, about +0.17, because informed traders buy whenever the sum is 26.

**Bid:** Any bid near fair value attracts informed sellers in the low-sum cases, where the sum averages about 15.7, and that loses heavily. I'll keep the bid low.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 26.1}

Card 1 is 11, so the settlement is 11 plus card 2. Card 2 is one of the 15 cards left: 2, 5, 6×3, 7, 8×4, 9×2, 13×3.

**Updating on the stage-1 trades:**
- **Quotes 1 and 2:** buyers took my ask at 21.5 and then at 23.5. An informed trader would only buy that high if the sum were 24, meaning card 2 is 13. Noise buyers that far above the stage-1 fair value (about 16.5) are rare, roughly 11%. So each buy is about 10 times more likely if the sum is 24.
- **Quote 3:** there was no trade between 14 and 26.1. That barely changes the picture.
- **Posterior:** about 3×100 weight on card 2 = 13, against roughly 12 for all the other cards. That puts P(sum = 24) at about 96%.
- **Fair value:** about 0.96 × 24 + 0.04 × 17.8 ≈ 23.7.

**Quote choice:** I am short 2.
- I put the ask just above 24, so an informed trader who knows the sum is 24 won't buy. Any noise buyers there are at least break-even.
- A bid around 22 picks up noise sellers at about a 2-point edge.
- The cost is a small risk that the sum is low and an informed trader sells to me.

{"bid": 22, "ask": 24.2}

Given card 1 = 11 and the trading history, settlement is almost certainly 24, so I'm centring my quote there and keeping it wide to earn from noise traders.

**Possible outcomes.** The 15 cards left are 2, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13. The settlement sum S = 11 + card 2 can therefore be 13, 16–20, or 24. Before using the history, the expected value is about 19.1.

**What the history implies.** The noise-trader probabilities below use estimated public fair values at each quote.
- **Quotes 1 and 2:** buyers took my asks at 21.5 and 23.5. With 11 as card 1, only S = 24 is above 23.5. An informed trader with any lower sum would not have bought at 23.5. A noise trader buys at 23.5 only about 14% of the time.
- **Quote 3:** no trade at 14 / 26.1. This is consistent with S = 24.
- **Quote 4:** no trade at 22 / 24.2. An informed trader with S below 22 would have sold at my bid of 22. The only informed trader who would do nothing at that quote is one who knows S = 24. A noise trader who doesn't trade explains the rest.
- **Posterior:** multiplying the likelihoods gives S = 24 a probability of about 99.4%. The fair value is about 24.0.

**Choosing the quote.**
- An informed trader who knows S = 24 will not trade if my bid is below 24 and my ask is above 24.
- Noise traders are now centred near 24 with a standard deviation of 4.1. The spread that maximises profit from them is roughly ±2.5.
- The remaining risk is small. An informed trader with a low sum (about 0.6% chance) could sell to me at 21.5, which would cost about 3.5 per unit.

{"bid": 21.5, "ask": 26.5}

The settlement value is almost certainly 24, so I quote symmetrically around 24.

**What the trading shows**
- With card 1 = 11, the remaining 15 cards average about 8.07. That puts the prior fair value near 19.1.
- In stage 1, counterparties bought at 21.5 and at 23.5. If the trader was informed, each buy means the sum is above the ask. Only a second card of 13 (sum 24) fits that.
- A noise trader buying that high was unlikely, roughly 9% each time. After both buys, sum = 24 has about 97% posterior weight.
- In stage 2, quote 4 (22 / 24.2) got no trade. An informed trader with sum 24 would not trade, but one with any lower sum would have sold at 22.
- Quote 5 (21.5 / 26.5) also got no trade, which again fits a sum of 24.
- The posterior is now above 99.8% on sum = 24, so fair value is about 24.0.

**Choosing the quote**
- An informed trader values the contract at exactly 24, so it will not trade if my bid is below 24 and my ask is above 24.
- Only noise traders (valuation about 24 + N(0, 4.1)) will trade.
- Expected profit per side is roughly d × P(noise > d), where d is the distance from 24. This is largest at about d ≈ 0.75 × 4.1 ≈ 3.1.
- My position of -2 leaves room to buy or sell one unit, so I quote both sides.

{"bid": 20.9, "ask": 27.1}

info.raw:
I'm setting a wide quote because the deal has heavy tails and informed traders will pick off anything tight.

**Prior value.** The deck averages 118/13 ≈ 9.08 per card, so the expected sum of 3 cards is about **27.2**. The standard deviation is about 7.8.

{"bid": 16.9, "ask": 37.0}

After the buy at 37, I estimate the fair value at about 35.2, so I'm quoting a low bid of 22 and an ask of 41.

**Prior.** The deck sums to 118 over 13 cards, so the expected sum of 3 cards is 3 × 118/13 ≈ 27.2.

**Update from the buy at 37.**
- A total above 37 needs one of four card combinations:
  - {14,14,13}: 4 ways
  - {14,14,10}: 3 ways
  - {14,13,13}: 12 ways
  - {13,13,13}: 4 ways
- That is 23 of 286 deals, a prior probability of about 0.080.
- If the total is above 37, the chance of a buy at 37 is about 0.52 (an informed trader always buys, plus a small chance from a noise trader).
- If it is not, only a noise trader buys, about 0.023. That needs noise above 9.8, which happens about 4.6% of the time, halved for the chance the counterparty is noise.
- So the posterior probability that the total is above 37 is about 0.66.
- If it is above 37, the expected value is about 39.7; otherwise about 26.1.
- The posterior fair value is about 35.2, with two clusters of outcomes.

**Ask.**
- No total exceeds 41, so an ask at 41 can never be lifted by an informed trader.
- A noise trader buys there with probability about 0.16, and I earn about 5.8 on that sale.
- That gives about +0.46 per quote. An ask at 40 earns about the same (+0.43).
- Asks lower than 40 lose more to informed buyers than they gain.
- My position is -1, so selling one more stays within the limit.

**Bid.**
- If an informed trader is behind the trade but the total is not above 37, the expected value is about 26.
- A bid near 30 would mostly be hit by informed sellers who know the value is low, so it loses money on average.
- I keep the bid low, where only a strongly negative noise draw would sell to me.

{"bid": 22, "ask": 41}

Fair value estimate: about 38.4. After card 1 (a 14), 12 cards remain and the next two cards average 17.3. On card values alone that gives a fair value of about 31.3.

The trading history pushes it up a lot:
- **Quote 1:** someone bought at 37 when the stage-1 fair value was only about 27.2. A noise trader does that only about 4.6% of the time. So it was very likely an informed buyer, meaning the settlement value is above 37.
- **Quote 2:** there was no trade at 22/41. That fits a value of 41 or less.

Weighting each possible two-card total by these trade likelihoods puts most of the probability on settlement values of 38, 40 or 41. That gives an expected value of about 38.4.

**Ask:**
- The highest possible settlement value is 41.
- An ask above 41 can never be lifted by an informed trader, so only noise traders buy there.
- I measured each price by expected edge against fair value, counting only the trades that happen. About 42.5 maximises noise-trader profit, at roughly +0.48 per quote.

**Bid:**
- About 89% of the posterior sits at 38 or above.
- A bid near fair value would mostly be hit by informed sellers holding the low outcomes (around 27–30), which costs money.
- A bid around 32 gives a small positive edge, about +0.19, after informed losses.

{"bid": 32, "ask": 42.5}

My estimate of the settlement value is about 39.2.

**Remaining cards.** Card 1 is 14, so 12 cards are left: four 2s, three 10s, four 13s and one 14. The total can be 18, 26, 29, 30, 34, 37, 38, 40 or 41. The highest possible total is 41.

**What the history tells me.**
- Quote 1: someone bought at 37. A noise trader rarely values above 37 (about 5% chance) when the stage-1 fair value is about 27.2. An informed trader buys whenever the total is above 37. So the trade makes totals of 38, 40 and 41 much more likely.
- Quotes 2 and 3: no trade. This fits totals between 32 and 41.

**Posterior.**
| Total | Probability |
|---|---|
| 38 | about 21% |
| 40 | about 42% |
| 41 | about 28% |
| 37 | about 4% |
| Below 37 | about 5% |

The posterior mean is about 39.2.

**Quote choice.**
- Ask: an informed trader never buys above 41, so any ask above 41 only trades with noise traders. Asks between 42 and 44 give about +0.45 to +0.5 expected per quote, and 43 sits in that flat optimum.
- Bid: a bid around 34–35 trades enough with noise traders to outweigh the small chance of an informed seller holding a low total. That is roughly +0.35 expected. Buying would also cover part of my short position.

{"bid": 34.5, "ask": 43}

With cards 1 and 2 revealed (14 + 13 = 27), the only unknown is card 3. The fair value is about 35.3, and I'm quoting 29 / 40.9 to sit at the edges of the possible outcomes.

**Possible settlement values.** The 11 cards left are four 2s, three 10s, three 13s and one 14. So the contract settles at:

| Card 3 | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 29 | 4/11 |
| 10 | 37 | 3/11 |
| 13 | 40 | 3/11 |
| 14 | 41 | 1/11 |

The expected value of card 3 is 91/11 ≈ 8.27, so the public fair value is about 35.27.

**Ask side.**
- **Ask 40.9:** an informed trader buys only if the value is 41, and loses me just 0.1. A noise trader buys about 16.6% of the time, earning me about 5.6. Expected edge is about +0.46.
- **Ask 39.9:** expected edge is about +0.43, slightly worse.
- **Ask 36.9:** informed traders would buy whenever the value is 37, 40 or 41. Expected result is about -0.3, so this loses money.

**Bid side.**
- **Bid 29.0:** no settlement value is below 29, so informed traders never sell to me. A noise trader sells about 14% of the time, earning me about 6.3. Expected edge is about +0.44.
- **Bid 30:** an informed trader sells whenever the value is 29, which drops the net to about +0.29.
- **Bids nearer fair value:** these get hit hard by informed sellers when the value is 29.

**Position.** I'm short 1, which is comfortably within the ±3 limit either way.

{"bid": 29.0, "ask": 40.9}

Card 1 (14) and card 2 (13) are revealed, so the known sum is 27. There are 11 cards left in the deck: four 2s, three 10s, three 13s and one 14. The settlement is therefore one of these:

| Card 3 | Probability | Settlement |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4/11 | 29 |
| 10 | 3/11 | 37 |
| 13 | 3/11 | 40 |
| 14 | 1/11 | 41 |

The expected settlement is 27 + 91/11 ≈ 35.27. I treat this as the public fair value that noise traders centre on, ignoring the small signal from earlier no-trade quotes.

With one quote left, I set each side to maximise expected one-shot profit. Each side has two parts: the loss when an informed trader picks it off, and the edge from noise traders whose valuation crosses it.

**Ask:**
- Quoting inside 37 (e.g. 36.9) gets bought by informed traders 7/11 of the time. That costs about 0.62, against about 0.32 earned from noise traders, so it loses money.
- At 41.0, informed traders never buy. Noise traders buy with probability about 0.16 at an edge of about 5.7, worth about 0.46 per quote.
- 40.9 is roughly equal, and 39.6 (the best price if there were only noise traders) nets only about 0.38.
- So ask = 41.0.

**Bid:**
- At 29.0, informed traders never sell, because a valuation of 29 is not below 29. Noise traders sell with probability about 0.14 at an edge of about 6.3, worth about 0.44.
- Raising the bid lets informed traders sell when card 3 is a 2 (4/11 of the time). At 29.5 that cost leaves a net of about 0.37.
- So bid = 29.0.

My position stays within limits either way, ending at -2 or 0.

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 10 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 0, 1 card worth 4, 3 cards worth 5, 1 card worth 7, 2 cards worth 11, 2 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The settlement value is the sum of 3 cards drawn from a 10-card deck.

**Fair value**
- The deck totals 78, so the mean card is 7.8.
- The expected sum of 3 cards is 3 × 7.8 = 23.4.

**Spread of outcomes**
- The variance of one card is 83.2 − 7.8² = 22.36.
- For 3 cards drawn without replacement, the variance of the sum is 3 × 22.36 × 7/9 ≈ 52.2, so the standard deviation is about 7.2.

**Choosing the half-spread (h)**
I used a normal approximation for the settlement value and compared profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders, per quote:

| h | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 1.60 | 1.65 | −0.05 |
| 8 | 1.11 | 0.98 | +0.13 |
| 9 | 0.86 | 0.74 | +0.12 |
| 10 | 0.64 | 0.54 | +0.10 |

The best half-spread is about 8 around the fair value of 23.4. That gives a bid of 15.4 and an ask of 31.4.

{"bid": 15.4, "ask": 31.4}

Card 1 is a 5, so the settlement value is 5 plus the sum of two cards drawn from the remaining nine: 0, 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15.

**Fair value:** The nine remaining cards sum to 73, so each averages 8.11. Two cards average 16.22, giving a fair value of 5 + 16.22 = 21.22.

**Settlement distribution:** There are 36 equally likely pairs. The possible settlement values are:
9, 10, 10, 12, 14, 14, 15, 16, 16, 16, 17, 17, 20, 20, 20, 20, 21, 21, 21, 21, 23, 23, 24, 24, 25, 25, 25, 25, 27, 27, 27, 31, 31, 31, 31, 35.

**Choosing each side:** For each candidate price, I weighed two things:
- The expected loss to an informed trader, who trades only when the true value is strictly beyond my price.
- The expected gain from a noise trader, whose valuation is 21.22 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 5.4.

**Ask side (net expected profit per quote):**

| Ask | Net |
|---|---|
| 30 | about +0.10 |
| 31 | about +0.12 (best) |
| 32 | about +0.08 |

At 31.0, an informed trader buys only when the value is 35, which has probability 1/36.

**Bid side (net expected profit per quote):**

| Bid | Net |
|---|---|
| 15 | about +0.10 |
| 14 | about +0.12 (best) |
| 13 | about +0.11 |

At 14.0, an informed trader whose value is exactly 14 will not sell, because the trade requires a strictly lower value.

{"bid": 14.0, "ask": 31.0}

Card 1 is a 5, so 9 cards remain: 0, 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15. Their sum is 73, so each unseen card averages about 8.11. The public fair value is 5 + 2 × 8.11 ≈ 21.2.

The settlement value is 5 plus the sum of two of those cards. I listed all 36 possible pairs to get the exact spread of outcomes. Most of the probability sits between 14 and 27, with a lower tail (9, 10, 10, 12) and an upper tail (31 four times, and 35).

For each candidate price I compared two things:
- **Noise traders:** what I expect to earn from them, given their valuation is 21.2 plus noise with standard deviation 5.4.
- **Informed traders:** what I expect to lose to them, using the exact list of outcomes.

**Ask side** (expected net gain per quote):

| Ask | Net gain |
|---|---|
| 27 | ≈ 0.08 |
| 29 | ≈ 0.10 |
| 31 | ≈ 0.12 (best) |
| 32 | ≈ 0.08 |

**Bid side** (expected net gain per quote):

| Bid | Net gain |
|---|---|
| 12 | ≈ 0.11 |
| 13 | ≈ 0.11 |
| 14 | ≈ 0.12 (best) |
| 15 | ≈ 0.10 |

I'll quote a bid of 14 and an ask of 31.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 31}

The third card decides settlement, so I priced around its value and set each side where the informed trader is least able to hurt me.

**Fair value.** Cards 1 and 2 (5 and 0) are gone. The 8 cards left are 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15. Settlement is 5 + 0 + card 3.

| Settlement | 9 | 10 | 12 | 16 | 20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/8 | 2/8 | 1/8 | 2/8 | 2/8 |

The expected settlement value is **14.125**. No trades so far, so the history adds almost nothing to this.

**Ask.** An informed trader only buys if the true value is above my ask. With the ask at exactly 20.0, it never buys, because 20 is the highest possible outcome.
- A noise trader buys when its valuation is above 20, which is 5.875 above fair value. That happens with probability about 0.138.
- Expected profit at 20.0 is 0.5 × 0.138 × 5.875 ≈ **+0.41**.

Lower asks do worse:
- At 19.9, an informed buyer appears when the value is 20, which costs a little. Net is about +0.40.
- At 18, net is about +0.21.
- At 16, net is negative.

**Bid.** An informed trader only sells if the true value is below my bid. With the bid at 9.0, it never sells, because 9 is the lowest possible outcome.
- A noise trader sells when its valuation is below 9, which is 5.125 under fair value. That happens with probability about 0.171.
- Expected profit at 9.0 is 0.5 × 0.171 × 5.125 ≈ **+0.44**.

Higher bids do worse:
- At 9.9, net is about +0.40.
- At 10.0, net is about +0.40.
- At 12, net is negative.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 20.0}

The fair value is 14.125. The best quote is bid 9 and ask 20, because the informed trader never trades at those prices.

**Fair value.** The revealed cards are 5 and 0, so the known sum is 5. Eight cards remain for card 3: 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15. Each is equally likely, so the settlement value can be 9, 10, 10, 12, 16, 16, 20 or 20.

Fair value = 5 + 73/8 = 14.125.

No trade happened at quote 5 (bid 9, ask 20). An informed trader would not have traded at those prices whatever card 3 was. So the lack of a trade tells us nothing, and the fair value stays at 14.125.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only if the settlement value is above the ask. A noise trader buys with probability 1 − Φ((ask − 14.125)/5.4), and I gain (ask − 14.125) on that trade.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 16 | about −0.16 |
| 19 | about +0.32 |
| 20 | about +0.41 |
| 21 | about +0.35 |

At 20 the informed trader never buys, since the maximum value is 20 and a tie does not trade.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only if the settlement value is below the bid. A noise trader sells with probability Φ((bid − 14.125)/5.4), and I gain (14.125 − bid) on that trade.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 12 | about −0.07 |
| 10 | about +0.40 |
| 9 | about +0.44 |
| 8 | about +0.39 |

At 9 the informed trader never sells, since the minimum value is 9 and a tie does not trade.

game.title: Card sum

info.raw:
The expected sum is about 12.23 and its standard deviation is about 6.0, so I'll quote roughly ±5.5 around 12.2.

**Fair value**
- The 13 cards sum to 53, so the mean card value is about 4.077.
- The expected sum of 3 cards is about 12.23.
- One card has variance of about 14.2.
- Because cards are dealt without replacement, the variance of the 3-card sum is 3 × 14.2 × (10/12) ≈ 35.6, so its standard deviation is about 6.0.

**Spread**
I compared the expected profit per quote at different half-spreads. Noise traders arrive 80% of the time and their valuations have standard deviation 8.9. Informed traders arrive 20% of the time and know the true value.
- At ±5, I expect to earn about 1.15 from noise traders and lose about 0.14 to informed ones.
- At ±6, the figures are about 1.2 and 0.1.

The net profit is fairly flat between ±5 and ±6. I've picked about ±5.5, partly because the two 12-value cards make the outcome lumpy and harder to predict.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 17.7}

Fair value is now about 13.7. I've skewed my quotes slightly upward because I'm short one unit.

**Prior fair value**
- The 13 cards sum to 53, so the average card is worth 53/13 ≈ 4.08.
- Three cards are dealt, so the expected sum is about 12.23.

**Update from the buy at 17.7**
- The settlement value is above 17.7 only if the sum is 18 or more. That needs at least one 12-card, since without a 12 the most you can reach is 14.
- That happens with probability 67/286 ≈ 0.234. When it does, the average sum is about 20.5. Otherwise the average sum is about 9.7.
- A noise trader values the contract at 12.23 plus noise with SD 8.9. It buys above 17.7 with probability 0.8 × 0.27 ≈ 0.215.
- An informed trader buys only if the sum is 18 or more, which adds 0.2 to the buy probability in that case.
- Weighting the two cases by how likely the buy was in each gives a posterior fair value of about 13.7.

**Quote**
- I'm short one unit, so I nudge both quotes slightly upward.
- The bid and ask are spread wide around 13.7. This protects against informed traders, especially the skewed upside from the 12-cards.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 18.5}

Card 1 = 12. The remaining 12 cards sum to 41, so before using the trade history the fair value is 12 + 2 × 41/12 ≈ 18.8.

**Adjusting for the stage-1 trade.** Someone bought at 17.7 when the prior fair value was about 12.2.
- An informed buyer only buys if the settlement is above 17.7. That means cards 2 and 3 sum to 6 or more, which holds in 39 of the 66 possible pairs.
- A noise trader buys with probability of about 0.27, whatever the cards are.
- So pairs summing to 6 or more get weight 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.27 ≈ 0.42. The other pairs get weight 0.8 × 0.27 ≈ 0.22.
- The high pairs average about 9.3 and the low pairs about 3.2.
- Weighting these gives an expected sum of about 7.7 for cards 2 and 3, so the fair value is about 19.7.

**Quote.** The remaining value is still quite uncertain, so I quote fairly wide around the fair value. I lean slightly toward buying because I am short 1.

{"bid": 16.8, "ask": 22.8}

The remaining deck holds 11 cards: 0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 6, 12. Their mean is 37/11 ≈ 3.36. The settlement is 16 plus card 3, so fair value is about 19.36. The possible outcomes are 16 (two cards), 17, 18 (three), 20 (three), 22 and 28.

**How each side was scored.** For each candidate price I added two parts:
- Noise traders (probability 0.8) trade with spread 8.9 around fair value. They earn me my distance from fair value whenever they hit the quote.
- The informed trader (probability 0.2) trades only when the true value is beyond my quote. Each outcome has a 1-in-11 chance.

**Ask side:**

| Ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 22 | about 0.70 |
| 24 | about 1.04 |
| 26 to 26.5 | about 1.18 (best) |

Above 22 the only informed buyer is when card 3 is the 12, so its cost is small.

**Bid side:**

| Bid | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 16 | about 0.95 (no informed seller loses me money) |
| 13 | about 1.21 |
| about 12.7 | about 1.21 (best) |

My position is -1 with two quotes left, so the ±3 limit doesn't constrain either side. I'm quoting a bid of 12.7 and an ask of 26.1.

{"bid": 12.7, "ask": 26.1}

With cards 12 and 4 known, the settlement is 16 plus the third card. That makes it 19.36 in expectation, so I quote **bid 12.7, ask 26.5**.

**Remaining deck and fair value.** After the 12 and the 4, eleven cards are left:
- two 0s and one 1
- three 2s and three 4s
- one 6 and one 12

These sum to 37, so card 3 averages 37/11 ≈ 3.36. The settlement is 16 + card 3, giving these outcomes:

| Settlement | 16 | 17 | 18 | 20 | 22 | 28 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 2/11 | 1/11 | 3/11 | 3/11 | 1/11 | 1/11 |

The public fair value is 19.36.

**What the last trade tells me.** Someone sold to me at 12.7. An informed trader would only sell below 12.7 if the value were under 12.7, and the minimum is 16. So that seller was a noise trader, and the trade carries no information.

**Bid.** At any bid at or below 16, informed traders never sell to me. The bid therefore only has to balance fill rate against edge on noise traders, whose valuations are N(19.36, 8.9).
- The best spacing is about 0.75 × 8.9 ≈ 6.7 below fair, so a bid near 12.7.
- That earns about 0.8 × 0.227 × 6.66 ≈ 1.21.
- For comparison, a bid of 16 earns only about 0.95.

**Ask.** The only informed buyer I can lose to is when the value is 28. I checked several ask levels:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 24 | ≈ 1.04 |
| 26 | ≈ 1.175 |
| 26.5 | ≈ 1.18 |
| 27 | ≈ 1.175 |
| 28 | ≈ 1.15 |

The ask is best at about 26.5.

{"bid": 12.7, "ask": 26.5}

info.raw:
The deck averages 51/11 ≈ 4.64 per card, so three cards have an expected sum of about 13.9. The sum depends mostly on how many 11s are dealt:

| 11s dealt | Probability | Typical sum |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | ≈ 34% | 4–9 (mean 6.75) |
| 1 | ≈ 51% | 15–17 |
| 2 | ≈ 15% | 24–25 |
| 3 | ≈ 0.6% | 33 |

Because the value clusters in separate groups, an informed trader only trades against me when the true sum is far from my price. I compared candidate quotes on two things. One is the edge I earn from noise traders, whose valuations are about 13.9 ± 6.2. The other is what I expect to lose to informed traders.

| Bid / ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 10 / 17 | ≈ 0.50 |
| 9 / 18 | ≈ 0.73 |
| 8 / 19 | ≈ 0.87 |
| 7 / 20 | ≈ 0.90 |

The best results come from roughly 7–8 on the bid and 19–20 on the ask. The bid sits in the upper part of the no-11 range, and the ask is below the two-11 range but above the one-11 range, whose maximum is 17. I'll quote in the middle of that zone.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 19.5}

Prior fair value is 3 × 51/11 ≈ 13.9. The last quote's no-trade barely moves it, to about 13.93.

**Where the settlement value can land**

The sum clusters by how many 11s are dealt:

| Number of 11s | Probability | Possible sums |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 34% | 4 to 9 |
| 1 | 51% | 13 to 17 |
| 2 or 3 | 15% | 22 to 25, or 33 |

There are no possible values between 9 and 13, or between 17 and 22.

**Choosing the quotes**

I set each price to maximise expected edge from noise traders minus expected losses to informed traders.

- **Ask:** Any ask from about 18 to 21 is only hit by informed traders when the value is 22 or more. Expected profit peaks near an ask of 19.5–20, at about +0.49 per quote.
- **Bid:** A bid just under 8 keeps informed sellers to values of 7 or less. Expected profit peaks around a bid of 7.8–7.9, at about +0.55 per quote. Bidding above 8 or 9 lets informed traders with those values sell to me, which costs more than the extra noise trades earn.

{"bid": 7.8, "ask": 19.6}

Card 1 is a 3, so 10 cards remain: one 0, three 2s, three 3s and three 11s. The expected sum of the last two cards is 9.6, so the fair value is 3 + 9.6 = 12.6.

**Settlement distribution.** There are 45 equally likely pairs for the last two cards. The settlement value splits into two clusters:
- **Low cluster (21 of 45 pairs):** 5 (3 pairs), 6 (3), 7 (3), 8 (9), 9 (3).
- **High cluster (24 of 45 pairs):** 14 (3), 16 (9), 17 (9), 25 (3).

**Ask side.** I compared the expected loss to informed buyers against the expected gain from noise buyers, with noise standard deviation 6.2 around 12.6.
- Any ask between 9 and 16 loses money, because informed traders buy whenever the true value is 14, 16 or 17.
- At about 17 to 18, only a settlement of 25 hurts me. The net edge there is about +0.5 per quote, and it peaks near 17.8.

**Bid side.** I did the same comparison for the bid.
- At 9 the net edge is about +0.38.
- At 8 it is about +0.55.
- At 7 it is about +0.60, and it is roughly flat at 6.5. Around 6.8 is best.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 17.8}

Card 1 is a 3, so I priced off the 10 cards still in the deck. The quotes below are each placed to give the best expected profit for that side.

**What's left in the deck (10 cards):** one 0, three 2s, three 3s and three 11s. The average card is 4.8.

**Fair value:** 3 + 2 × 4.8 = **12.6**.

**Distribution of the settlement value:** it is 3 plus two of the remaining cards, which gives 45 equally likely pairs.

| Settlement | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 14 | 16 | 17 | 25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pairs (of 45) | 3 | 3 | 3 | 9 | 3 | 3 | 9 | 9 | 3 |

The value is bimodal. It lands at 5–9 with probability 21/45, at 14–17 with 21/45, and at 25 with 3/45.

**How I compared quotes:** for each candidate price, I set the expected loss to informed traders against the expected gain from noise traders. Noise traders value the contract at 12.6 plus normal noise with standard deviation 6.2.

**Ask side:**
- At 16.1 or below, informed traders buy whenever the value is 17 (9/45) or 25. That costs too much.
- Above 17, an informed buyer only appears when the value is 25.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 16.1 | ≈ 0.38 |
| 17.1 | ≈ 0.50 |
| 18.0 | ≈ 0.51 |
| 19.0 | ≈ 0.49 |

The best ask is about **18.0**.

**Bid side:**

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 9.1 | ≈ 0.36 |
| 8.1 | ≈ 0.53 |
| 7.0 | ≈ 0.60 |
| 6.1 | ≈ 0.60 |

Expected profit is flat at about 0.60 between bids of 6.1 and 7.0. I'll bid **7.0**.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 18.0}

The fair value is 11, and I'm quoting a bid of 6.0 and an ask of 17.1.

**Fair value.** Cards 1 and 2 are both 3, so the sum so far is 6. Nine cards remain: one 0, three 2s, two 3s and three 11s. The final sum is therefore 6, 8, 9 or 17, with probabilities 1/9, 3/9, 2/9 and 3/9. The expected third card is 45/9 = 5, so fair value is 11. The earlier quotes drew no trades, which tells us very little, so I've ignored them.

**Ask.** If my ask is below 17, an informed trader buys whenever the sum is 17 (probability 1/3). That costs me about 0.117 × (17 − ask) in expected loss. Setting the ask just above 17 removes that loss completely. Noise traders still buy about 16% of the time, giving an expected profit of about 0.645 per quote. That beats any ask in the 15–17 range, so I'll quote 17.1.

**Bid.** A bid of 6.0 is the lowest possible sum, so an informed trader never sells to me there. Noise traders sell about 21% of the time, for an expected profit of about 0.68. Raising the bid lets informed traders sell when the sum is 6 or 8, which lowers the expected profit:
- Bid 7: about 0.64
- Bid 8: about 0.54

So 6.0 is the best bid.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 17.1}

With cards 1 and 2 both revealed as 3, the sum so far is 6. I priced the contract at fair value 11 and quoted where my expected profit was highest.

**What card 3 can be.** The 9 cards left are one 0, three 2s, two 3s and three 11s. So the settlement value has four possible outcomes:

| Card 3 | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 6 | 1/9 |
| 2 | 8 | 3/9 |
| 3 | 9 | 2/9 |
| 11 | 17 | 3/9 |

The expected settlement is 6 + 45/9 = 11, which I used as the public fair value. I ignored the no-trade history, which carries little information.

**Choosing the ask.**
- At 17.0, an informed trader with a value of 17 is not strictly above my ask, so I never sell to one at a loss.
- Noise traders buy about 16.7% of the time, giving an expected profit of 0.65 × 0.167 × 6 ≈ 0.65.
- A lower ask such as 16 earns about 0.57, because informed buyers at 17 then cost me money.
- A higher ask earns less: 17.1 gives about 0.645 and 18 about 0.59.

**Choosing the bid.**
- At 6.0, an informed trader with a value of 6 is not strictly below my bid, so I never buy from one at a loss.
- Noise traders sell about 21% of the time, giving an expected profit of 0.65 × 0.21 × 5 ≈ 0.68.
- A bid of 7 earns about 0.64, a bid of 8 about 0.53, and a bid of 5.5 about 0.67.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 17.0}

info.raw:
The expected sum is about 17.5, but the outcome is lumpy: about 29% chance of no high card (sum about 5–11), about 50% chance of one (about 14–22), and about 20% chance of two or more (26 and up). Informed traders would pick off any tight quote, so I quote wide. Near 8–9, a bid is slightly profitable because noise sellers outweigh informed sellers with very low sums. On the ask side, every level breaks even or loses money, so I keep the ask far out.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 30}

Bid 7.5 / ask 32: no edge on the ask side, so I quote only a token ask; the low bid is the one with small positive expected value.

**Fair value.** The deck totals 76, so each card averages about 5.85. The expected sum of 3 cards is about 17.5, with a standard deviation of about 8. The no-trade at 8.5 / 30 barely moves this.

**Shape of the settlement.** It depends on how many 14s are dealt:
- **No 14s (about 42%):** usually a low sum, roughly 5 to 11, or about 16 if the 11 is dealt.
- **One 14 (about 47%):** usually about 17 to 22, or about 27 to 30 if the 11 is dealt.
- **Two 14s (about 10%):** about 29 to 39.

**Ask side.** Noise traders' valuations spread only about 6 around fair value. So any ask below about 30 loses more to informed buyers, who exploit the high tail, than it earns from noise traders. At an ask of about 32 both effects are close to zero, so it is effectively a placeholder.

**Bid side.** Sums below 8 are rare: 5 (about 2%), 6 (about 6%) and 7 (about 7%). A bid around 7 to 8 gives an informed seller only about 0.05 to 0.12 per quote. Meanwhile it earns about 0.2 to 0.27 from noise sellers. The expected net is slightly positive, roughly the same across that range, so I take 7.5.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 32}

Card 1 is a 3, so 12 cards remain, summing to 73. The expected settlement is 3 + 2 × 73/12 ≈ 15.17. Stage 1 had no trades, so the trading history tells us almost nothing.

The final value is lumpy:
- **Both remaining cards low:** settlement is between 6 and 11 (28 of 66 pairs).
- **One low, one high:** settlement is between 15 and 22 (32 of 66 pairs).
- **Both high:** settlement is 28 or 31 (6 of 66 pairs).

For each candidate price I weighed two effects. An informed trader only trades when it profits, so it costs me. A noise trader's valuation is about 15.17 ± 6, so it pays me the spread.

**Ask side:**
- At an ask of 22, only the outcomes of 28 or 31 hurt me. The informed loss is about 0.34 and the noise gain is about 0.43, so the net is roughly +0.09.
- Asks around 22–23 come out best. Lower asks, such as 18, lose money overall.

**Bid side:**
- At a bid of 7, only the four pairs that give a settlement of 6 hurt me. The informed loss is about 0.03 and the noise gain is about 0.35, so the net is roughly +0.32.
- Bids around 7–8 come out best.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 22.0}

Card 1 is a 3, so 12 cards remain, summing to 73. The expected settlement is 3 + 2 × 73/12 ≈ 15.17.

**How the settlement value is spread**
- **Both remaining cards low** (28 of 66 pairs): settlement is 6 to 11.
- **One low and one high card** (32 pairs): settlement is 15 to 22.
- **Both high** (6 pairs): settlement is 28 or 31.

**Choosing the bid**
- At a bid of 7, the expected loss to informed sellers is about 0.03.
- Noise traders (fair value 15.17, standard deviation 6) sell below 7 about 8.7% of the time, giving an expected gain of about 0.36 per quote.
- Net is about +0.32, which is roughly the best of the levels I checked.

**Choosing the ask**
- At an ask of 22, informed buyers only trade when both cards are high (settlement 28 or 31), costing about 0.34 in expectation.
- Noise buyers above 22 give an expected gain of about 0.43.
- Net is about +0.09, the best of the levels I checked.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 22}

**Fair value now.** Cards 1 and 2 sum to 5, so settlement is 5 plus card 3. The 11 cards left in the deck are 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5, 11, 14, 14, 14.

Possible settlements:

| Settlement | 6 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 16 | 19 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/11 | 3/11 | 2/11 | 1/11 | 1/11 | 3/11 |

The public fair value is about 5 + 71/11 ≈ 11.45, and noise traders value the contract at roughly N(11.45, 6).

**Ask side.**
- At an ask of 19, an informed trader never buys, because it only buys if the value is strictly above my ask.
- A noise trader buys with probability about 0.10, earning me about 7.55 per trade. That is roughly +0.39 per quote.
- Lower asks, such as 16 to 18, let informed traders buy when the value is 19 and score worse.

**Bid side.**
- At a bid of 6, an informed trader never sells, because it only sells if the value is strictly below my bid.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 0.18, earning me about 5.45 per trade. That is roughly +0.50 per quote.
- A bid of 7 picks up more noise trades but loses to informed traders when the value is 6, and comes out worse.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 19}

The third card is the only unknown left. I picked the quote that maximises expected profit from each side separately.

**Remaining deck (11 cards):** 1×1, 3×2, 2×3, 1×5, 1×11, 3×14.

**Possible settlement values:** the revealed cards sum to 3 + 2 = 5, so settlement = 5 + card 3.

| Settlement | 6 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 16 | 19 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/11 | 3/11 | 2/11 | 1/11 | 1/11 | 3/11 |

The public fair value is 5 + 71/11 ≈ 11.45. The earlier no-trade outcomes tell us nothing, because no informed trader could have traded at those quotes.

**Ask side:**
- Any ask below 19 is lifted by informed traders when settlement is 19, which happens with probability 3/11.
- An ask of exactly 19 is never lifted by an informed trader, since they only buy when their value is strictly above the ask.
- At 19, noise traders lift about 10.4% of the time, for an expected gain of about +0.39.
- An ask of 16 gains more from noise traders but loses about 0.41 to informed traders, netting only about +0.10.
- An ask of 20 earns about +0.33.
- So 19 is the best ask.

**Bid side:**
- A bid of exactly 6 is never hit by an informed trader.
- At 6, noise traders hit about 18% of the time, for an expected gain of about +0.50.
- A bid of 6.5 nets about +0.48, and a bid of 7 nets about +0.46.
- So 6 is the best bid.

Fair value is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25. The product is skewed: its standard deviation is about 8.9, and the upper tail is long while the lower tail stops at 1.

For each candidate price I compared two things:
- **Gain from noise traders:** 0.8 × the chance their valuation clears my price × my edge over 12.25.
- **Loss to informed traders:** 0.2 × the expected amount by which the true value beats my price.

**Ask side.** Net expected profit rises as the ask moves up, then levels off:

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 17 | about 0.94 |
| 19 | about 1.31 |
| 21 | about 1.51 |
| 23 | about 1.58 |
| 24.1 | about 1.58 |

I'll use 23.

**Bid side.** A low bid gives informed traders very little to exploit, because the product rarely falls below 3:

| Bid | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 6 | about 1.43 |
| 5 | about 1.58 |
| 4 | about 1.68 |
| 3 | about 1.75 |
| 2 | about 1.76 |

Bids of 2 and 3 are essentially tied, so I'll use 3.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 23}

Unconditionally, the expected product of two dice is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25. Quote 1 had no trade, which tells us little, so fair value stays at about 12.25.

**Ask side.** For each ask I weighed the expected gain from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders. The informed loss is 0.2 × E[(V − ask)⁺], where V is the settlement value.

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 20 | ≈ 1.44 |
| 22 | ≈ 1.56 |
| 23 | ≈ 1.58 |
| 24 | ≈ 1.58 |

The curve is flat around 23–24.

**Bid side.** I applied the same trade-off to the bid. The product's distribution has little mass at low values, so the informed risk is small there.

| Bid | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4 | ≈ 1.68 |
| 3 | ≈ 1.75 |
| 2.5 | ≈ 1.76 |

The optimum is around 2.5–3, so I keep a wide, slightly skewed quote.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 23}

Die 1 is 6, so the contract settles at 6 × die 2. That means one of {6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36}, each equally likely, with a fair value of 21.

**How I chose the quotes:**
- Each side earns from noise traders: 0.8 × P(noise trade) × edge. Noise traders value the contract at about N(21, 13²).
- Each side loses to informed traders: 0.2 × the average shortfall against the settlement values beyond my quote.

**Ask (expected value per quote):**

| Ask | Net EV |
|---|---|
| 30 | ≈ 1.56 |
| 31 | ≈ 1.60 |
| 32 | ≈ 1.62 |
| 33 | ≈ 1.61 |

The ask peaks around 32, where the only informed loss is when the settlement is 36.

**Bid:** The game is symmetric around 21, so the best bid is about 10. The only informed loss there is when the settlement is 6.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 32}

The fair value is about 18.4, so I'll quote a bid of 6 and an ask of 30.

- At quote 3 someone sold to me at my bid of 10.

  - A noise trader sells if its valuation, 21 plus noise, is below 10. The chance of that is about 0.199.
- So the chance of that sale is about 0.359 if the value is 6, and about 0.159 for every other value.
- Updating on the sale gives these chances: 6 is about 0.31, and each of the other values is about 0.138.
- The fair value is therefore about **18.4**.

**Choosing the quotes**
I picked each side to maximise expected profit against noise traders (fair value plus noise with standard deviation 13) and informed traders.
- **Ask:**

  - At 30, only a settlement value of 36 lets an informed buyer beat me.
- **Bid:**
  - Expected profit is highest at 6, at about 1.69.

game.title: Dice/cards count
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 4, 7, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dice showing at least 6.

info.raw:
Fair value comes from the chance each die shows 6 or more.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 shows 7 or 8 with probability 1/2.
- Die 2 shows 10, 11, 12, 12 or 12 with probability 5/8.
- Expected value = 10 × (0.5 + 0.625) = **11.25**.
- Settlement distribution:
  - Value 0 has probability 0.1875.
  - Value 10 has probability 0.5.
  - Value 20 has probability 0.3125.

**Choosing the edges**

For each side, I weigh what I earn from noise traders against what I lose to informed traders.
- Noise traders hit my quote with probability P(Z > s/7), where s is the distance from fair value. Each such trade earns s.
- Informed traders hit my ask only when the value is 20, which has probability 0.3125. They hit my bid only when the value is 0, which has probability 0.1875.

Ask side, expected profit per quote is 0.8·P(Z > s/7)·s − 0.2·0.3125·(8.75 − s):

| s | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 5 | 0.72 |
| 6 | 0.77 |
| 7 | 0.78 (best) |
| 7.5 | 0.77 |

The best edge is about 7, so the ask is about 18.3.

Bid side, expected profit per quote is 0.8·P(Z > s/7)·s − 0.2·0.1875·(11.25 − s):

| s | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 5 | 0.72 |
| 6 | 0.74 (best) |
| 7 | 0.73 |

The best edge is about 6, so the bid is about 5.2.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 18.3}

Settlement is 10 × (number of dice showing ≥6), so I priced each side by trading off noise-trader profit against losses to informed traders.

**Prior.**
- Die 1 shows ≥6 (a 7 or 8) with probability 1/2.
- Die 2 shows ≥6 (10, 11 or one of the three 12s) with probability 5/8.
- So the settlement is 0 with probability 3/16, 10 with probability 8/16, and 20 with probability 5/16. The mean is 11.25.

**Update after no trade at 5.2 / 18.3.**
- A noise trader (valuation 11.25 plus noise with standard deviation 7) would not trade about 65% of the time.
- An informed trader knowing the value is 10 would never trade at those prices. Informed traders knowing 0 or 20 would always trade.
- So no trade shifts weight toward 10. The posterior is about 0.157 for 0, 0.581 for 10 and 0.262 for 20.
- The new fair value is about 11.05.

**Choosing the ask.** Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 11.05) − 0.2 × 0.262 × (20 − ask).

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 16 | 0.74 |
| 17 | 0.785 |
| 17.5 | 0.79 |
| 18 | 0.785 |
| 19 | 0.76 |

The best ask is about 17.5.

**Choosing the bid.** Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise valuation < bid) × (11.05 − bid) − 0.2 × 0.157 × bid.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4 | 0.76 |
| 4.5 | 0.774 |
| 5 | 0.78 |
| 5.5 | 0.777 |

The best bid is about 5.0.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 17.5}

Die 1 shows 4, so it adds nothing to settlement. Only die 2 matters. Die 2 is at least 6 on 5 of its 8 faces (10, 11, 12, 12, 12), so settlement is 10 with probability 5/8 and 0 with probability 3/8. The public fair value is 6.25.

**Ask:** An informed trader only buys if the value (10) is above my ask. With an ask of 10 or more, informed traders never hit it. Noise traders buy when their valuation, 6.25 plus Normal noise with sd 7, exceeds my ask.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 9 | 0.64 (includes about 0.125 expected loss to informed buyers) |
| 10 | 0.89 |
| 11 | 0.95 |
| 12 | 0.95 |
| 13 | 0.91 |

The best ask is around 11.7.

**Bid:** An informed trader only sells if the value (0) is below my bid. With a bid of 0, informed traders never sell to me. Noise traders sell when their valuation is below my bid.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| -0.5 | 0.91 |
| 0 | 0.93 |
| 0.5 | 0.91 |
| 1 | 0.88 |

The best bid is 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 11.7}

Die 1 showed 4, so the contract settles at 10 only if die 2 shows at least 6. Die 2 does that on 5 of its 8 faces (10, 11, 12, 12, 12), so the settlement is either 10 or 0 and the fair value is 6.25.

**Last trade.** The buy at 11.7 tells us nothing, because an informed trader can value the contract at 10 at most and would not pay 11.7. So the fair value stays 6.25.

**Ask.**
- Any ask below 10 gets lifted by an informed buyer whenever the value is 10, which loses money.
- At 10 or above, only noise traders buy. Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise > ask) × (ask − 6.25).
- This peaks around an ask of 12, at about 0.95 per quote.

**Bid.**
- Any bid above 0 gets hit by an informed seller whenever the value is 0.
- At a bid of 0, only noise traders sell, giving about 0.93 expected profit.

game.description:

info.raw:
The expected settlement value is 11.67. I set each side of the quote by trading off profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders.

**Settlement distribution**
- Die 1 shows at least 7 (faces 7, 8, 10, 12) with probability 2/3.
- Die 2 shows at least 7 (faces 8, 9) with probability 3/10 + 1/5 = 1/2.
- The contract is worth 0 with probability 1/3 × 1/2 = 1/6.
- It is worth 10 with probability 2/3 × 1/2 + 1/3 × 1/2 = 1/2.
- It is worth 20 with probability 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3.
- Expected value = 10 × (2/3 + 1/2) = **11.67**.

**Ask side**
- Per quote, expected profit = 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 11.67), minus the expected loss to informed traders.
- An informed trader buys only if the true value is strictly above the ask.
- At an ask of exactly 20.0, an informed trader holding a value of 20 does not trade, so there is no informed loss.
- Expected profit at an ask of 20 is about 1.10, the best of the asks tested:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 15 | 0.22 |
| 17 | 0.68 |
| 19 | 0.99 |
| 20 | 1.10 |
| 21 | 1.06 |

**Bid side**
- Any bid above 0 can be hit by an informed trader when the value is 0 (probability 1/6).
- Expected profit at a bid of 1–2 is about 0.93:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.92 |
| 1 | 0.93 |
| 2 | 0.93 |
| 3 | 0.91 |
| 10 | −0.11 (loses money) |

- I set the bid at 1.5, between the two best values.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 20.0}

The current fair value is about 12.6, so I'll quote a bid of 4 and an ask of 20.

**Prior distribution of the settlement value**
- Die 1 shows at least 7 (faces 7, 8, 10, 12) with probability 4/6 = 2/3.
- Die 2 shows at least 7 (faces 8 and 9) with probability 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5.
- So the settlement is 0 with probability 1/6, 10 with probability 1/2, and 20 with probability 1/3.
- The prior mean is about 11.67.

**What quote 1's "no trade" tells us**
- An informed trader with value 0 would have sold at my bid of 1.5, so no trade makes value 0 less likely.
- An informed trader with value 20 does not buy at exactly 20, so it would also not have traded.
- A noise trader fails to trade with probability about 0.64.
- Updating on that, the posterior is about 0.10 on 0, 0.54 on 10 and 0.36 on 20.
- That gives a fair value of about 12.6.

**Choosing the quote**
- **Ask:** An ask of exactly 20 never loses to an informed trader. It still earns about 1.1 in expected profit from noise buyers. Asking lower adds some noise profit but loses more to informed traders whose value is 20.
- **Bid:** Any bid above 0 loses to informed traders whose value is 0, but that probability is small, about 0.035. I compared bids of 0, 2, 4 and 5. A bid of about 4 has the best expected profit, around 0.95.

{"bid": 4, "ask": 20}

Die 2 = 9 counts as one die at 7 or more, so the contract settles at 10 or 20. Die 1 shows 7 or more with probability 4/6 = 2/3 (faces 7, 8, 10, 12). Public fair value is 10 + 20 × 2/3 ≈ 16.67. The stage 1 no-trades told us nothing about die 1.

**Ask side.** An ask of 20 or higher means the informed trader never buys, because the most it can value the contract at is 20. Only noise traders buy then, which is pure edge. Expected profit is 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 16.67):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 22 | about 1.03 |
| 24 | about 1.10 |
| 25 | about 1.10 |

**Bid side.** A bid at or below 10 means the informed trader never sells, because the least it can value the contract at is 10. Expected profit from noise sellers is 0.65 × P(noise valuation < bid) × (16.67 − bid):

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 8.5 to 9 | about 1.10 |
| 10 | about 1.09 |
| 11 | about 0.93 (the informed trader at value 10 now sells to us) |

I'll quote bid 9 and ask 24.5.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 24.5}

With die 2 revealed as 9, the fair value is about 16.67, and that is unchanged by the trade at quote 3.

**Fair value**
- Die 2 shows 9, which is at least 7, so it adds 10 for certain.
- Die 1 is at least 7 with probability 4/6 (faces 7, 8, 10, 12).
- So settlement is 20 with probability 2/3 and 10 with probability 1/3. Fair value is about 16.67.

**The quote-3 trade carries no information.** The settlement value can only be 10 or 20, so an informed trader would never buy at 24.5. The buyer must have been a noise trader, and fair value stays at about 16.67.

**Ask**
- Any ask at or above 20 means informed traders never buy from me.
- Against noise traders (fair value plus noise with sd 10), expected profit is (a − 16.67) × P(valuation > a). This peaks about 0.75 sd above fair value, at roughly 24.2.

**Bid**
- Any bid at or below 10 means informed traders never sell to me.
- The same calculation for noise sellers puts the best bid about 0.75 sd below fair value, at roughly 9.2. That is under 10, so informed traders are excluded.
- I checked bids just above 10, and they do slightly worse. At 10.5 the expected profit is about 1.02, against about 1.105 at 9.2.

My position is −1, so both sides are allowed.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 24.2}

game.contract: The contract settles at the product of the two dice.

info.raw:
Before any reveal, the fair value is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25. The product is lumpy and right-skewed, ranging from 1 to 36 with a standard deviation of about 8.9.

**What each side earns.** A trade with a noise trader earns me the gap between my price and 12.25. A trade with an informed trader (probability 0.35) loses me whatever the true value is beyond my price. I checked a few prices on each side using the exact distribution of the product.

**Ask side:**

| Ask | Expected informed loss | Expected noise gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 17 | about 0.73 | about 0.74 | about 0 |
| 20 | about 0.48 | about 0.62 | about +0.15 |
| 22 | about 0.36 | about 0.46 | about +0.10 |

The ask is best at about 20.

**Bid side:**

| Bid | Expected informed loss | Expected noise gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | about 0.54 | about 0.73 | about +0.19 |
| 6 | about 0.26 | about 0.71 | about +0.45 |
| 5 | about 0.17 | about 0.66 | about +0.49 |
| 4 | about 0.09 | about 0.59 | about +0.50 |

The bid side is flat between 4 and 5, so I'll bid 4.5. The bid sits further from fair value than the ask because the low end of the distribution is dense.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 20.0}

Unconditionally, the product of two fair dice has an expected value of 3.5² = 12.25 and a wide spread (standard deviation about 8.9).

**Update from quote 1.** Nobody traded at 4.5 / 20. That is somewhat more likely when the true value lies between 5 and 20, so I pull my estimate slightly toward the middle. The updated fair value is about **12.0**.

**Choosing each side.** For each candidate price, I compare two things:
- the expected gain from noise traders (65% of arrivals, valuation = fair value + noise with standard deviation 6.7);
- the expected loss to informed traders (35% of arrivals, who trade only when the true value is beyond my price).

| Side | Price | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ask | 17 | 0.74 | 0.73 | ≈ 0 |
| Ask | 19 | 0.68 | 0.55 | ≈ +0.13 |
| Ask | 21 | 0.53 | 0.42 | ≈ +0.11 |
| Bid | 7 | 0.74 | 0.40 | ≈ +0.34 |
| Bid | 6 | 0.71 | 0.26 | ≈ +0.45 |
| Bid | 5 | 0.68 | 0.17 | ≈ +0.51 |
| Bid | 4.5 | 0.64 | 0.17 | ≈ +0.47 |

The bid side is more attractive because the distribution has a long upper tail. That makes informed buying costly, while low outcomes are bounded near 1.

I'll bid 5.0, which scores best. On the ask, 19 and 21 are close, so I'll use 19.5.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 19.5}

The public fair value is about 12.25, since each die has mean 3.5 and the dice are independent. The two quotes with no trade tell us little.

The settlement distribution is skewed: most products are small, but there is a long right tail (24, 25, 30, 36). I weighed the expected profit from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders on each side:

- **Ask side:** an ask near 20 nets about +0.15 per quote. Lower asks lose too much to informed buyers when the product is 18 or more.
- **Bid side:** bids between 4 and 5 net about +0.50 per quote. Informed sellers only hurt us on the few very small products.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 20}

Die 1 is 3, so the contract settles at 3 × (die 2). That means one of 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18, each equally likely, with a fair value of 10.5.

**Ask side.** I compared expected profit at several asks:

| Ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 15 | about 0.56 |
| 16 | about 0.62 |
| 17 | about 0.643 |
| 17.5 | about 0.644 |
| 18 | about 0.64 |

At 17.5:
- An informed counterparty only buys if the value is 18. That has a 1/6 chance and loses me 0.5, for an expected cost of about 0.03.
- A noise trader buys about 15% of the time and earns me 7 when it does. That is worth about 0.67.
- Net, the ask is worth about 0.64.

**Bid side.** The possible values are symmetric around 10.5, so the best bid mirrors the ask at 3.5.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 17.5}

With die 1 revealed as 3, the contract settles at 3 × die 2, so the possible values are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 or 18.

**Updating on the last trade.** Before quote 4 the fair value was 10.5 (3 × 3.5). Someone then sold to me at 3.5.
- An informed trader sells at 3.5 only if the value is 3.
- A noise trader sells at 3.5 with probability Φ((3.5 − 10.5)/6.7) = Φ(−1.045) ≈ 0.148.
- So the chance of that sale was 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.148 ≈ 0.446 if the value is 3, and 0.65 × 0.148 ≈ 0.096 otherwise.

**Posterior.**
- P(value = 3) ≈ 0.48.
- Each of 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18 has probability ≈ 0.104.
- Public fair value ≈ 0.48 × 3 + 0.104 × 60 ≈ 7.67.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared expected profit at several ask levels:

| Ask | Gain from noise buyers | Loss to informed buyers | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | +0.73 | −0.33 | ≈ +0.40 |
| 14 | +0.71 | −0.18 | ≈ +0.53 |
| 14.9 | +0.66 | −0.12 | ≈ +0.54 |
| 17.9 | +0.42 | ≈ 0 | ≈ +0.42 |

An ask of 14.9 is best. Selling also trims my long position.

**Choosing the bid.** At 5.9 the loss to informed sellers when the value is 3 outweighs the noise gain, giving about −0.03. At 2.9 no informed trader will ever sell to me, since the lowest possible value is 3. The noise gain there is 0.65 × 0.238 × 4.77 ≈ +0.74, so I bid 2.9.

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 14.9}

The last move fixes this quote: die 1 = 3, so the contract settles at 3 × die 2, one of {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}.

**Updating on the trades so far**
- **Quote 4: someone sold to me at 3.5.**
  - An informed trader sells there only if the value is 3. That happens with probability 0.35, plus 0.65 × about 0.15 from noise traders.
  - For any other value, only a noise trader sells.
  - After this, the chance the value is 3 is about 48%. Each of the other five values is about 10.4%.
- **Quote 5: no trade at 2.9 / 14.9.**
  - An informed trader would have bought if the value were 15 or 18. No trade makes those two values less likely.
  - The updated chances are: 3 at about 0.53; 6, 9 and 12 at about 0.115 each; 15 and 18 at about 0.06 each.
  - Public fair value is about 6.7.

**Choosing the quote**
- **Ask:** the gain from noise traders buying above fair value outweighs the loss to informed traders when the value is 15 or 18. Expected profit is highest at about 0.56, with the ask near 13.
- **Bid:** a bid below 3 means no informed trader ever sells to me. Only noise traders hit it, and they do so below fair value. Expected profit is highest at about 0.74, with the bid near 2.

game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
I'm quoting a bid of 1.0 and an ask of 9.0. Both sides earn a small positive expected profit.

**Settlement distribution.** There are C(12,3) = 220 equally likely hands. The contract settles at the smallest card dealt:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 1 | 55/220 ≈ 25% |
| 3 | 130/220 ≈ 59% |
| 9 | 31/220 ≈ 14% |
| 14 | 4/220 ≈ 2% |

The expected value is 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Bid.** Any bid above 1 lets an informed trader who knows the value is 1 sell to me at a loss to me. Bidding exactly 1.0 means they don't sell, because they only sell below my bid. Noise traders still sell to me at 1.0 often enough to earn about +0.23 per quote. Raising the bid toward 2 adds more noise trades but loses more to informed sellers, so the edge shrinks.

**Ask.** Asking near 3–5 gets bought by informed traders whenever the value is 9 or 14, which is very costly. At 9.0, only an informed trader who knows the value is 14 buys. Noise traders buying above 9 roughly offset that, for a slight positive edge.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Quoting bid 1.0 and ask 8.9: the fair value is about 3.44, and the quotes sit just inside the values an informed trader would trade on.

**Distribution of the minimum card** (220 possible 3-card hands):
- Minimum is 1: 55/220
- Minimum is 3: 130/220
- Minimum is 9: 31/220
- Minimum is 14: 4/220

The prior expected value is 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Update from quote 1 (bid 1, ask 9, no trade):** If the minimum were 14, an informed trader would have bought at 9, so "no trade" makes 14 less likely. After this update, fair value is about 3.44. The settlement values are 1, 3, 9 or 14, with probabilities of roughly 0.25, 0.60, 0.14 and 0.01.

**Ask side:**
- Anywhere between 3 and 9, an informed trader buys whenever the minimum is 9 or 14, so I lose to them.
- An ask just under 9 keeps that loss small, and noise traders still occasionally pay a lot more than fair value.
- At 8.9 the expected profit is about +0.04, against about 0 at an ask of 6.

**Bid side:**
- If I bid above 1, I lose to informed traders whenever the minimum is 1.
- At exactly 1, an informed trader with value 1 does not sell (1 is not below 1), but noise traders below 1 still sell to me.
- Expected profit is about +0.23 at a bid of 1, against about +0.09 at 2, so 1.0 is best.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 8.9}

The first card is a 9, so the settlement is at most 9. The other 11 cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s, and two of them are still to come.

**Distribution of the minimum** (55 equally likely pairs):
- P(min = 1) = 10/55 ≈ 0.18
- P(min = 3) = 30/55 ≈ 0.55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55 ≈ 0.27
- Fair value ≈ 235/55 ≈ 4.27

**Ask side:** An informed buyer only appears if the value is 9. An ask of exactly 9.0 never trades with an informed buyer. Noise buyers above 9 still give about +0.11 expected profit. Any ask below 9 loses more to informed buyers than it gains from extra noise trades.

**Bid side:** An informed seller only appears if the value is 1. A bid of exactly 1.0 never trades with an informed seller. Noise sellers below 1 give about +0.20 expected profit. Bids of 1.5 to 3 earn less, because selling at a value of 1 costs too much.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Fair value given card 1 = 9 is about 4.27, so I'll quote bid 1 and ask 9, the same as last time.

**Fair value.** The remaining 11 cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. Two more cards are dealt.
- P(min = 1) = 10/55
- P(min = 3) = 30/55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55
- Expected value = (10 + 90 + 135)/55 ≈ 4.27

**Ask.** An informed trader only buys if its value is above my ask. At 9, even a true value of 9 does not buy, so only noise traders hit it, and they pay well above fair value. Lowering the ask below 9 lets informed traders buy when the value is 9. That costs more than the extra noise flow brings in. Raising it above 9 loses noise flow, so 9 is best.

**Bid.** An informed trader only sells if its value is below my bid. At 1, even a true value of 1 does not sell, so only noise traders hit it. Raising the bid above 1 lets informed traders sell when the value is 1, which costs more than the extra noise flow gains. Bid 1 is about optimal, with expected profit around 0.20.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

Card 2 is the only 1 in the deck, so the minimum of the dealt cards is already 1. Settlement is certain to be **1**, and the public fair value is 1.

- **Informed traders** value the contract at exactly 1. With bid ≤ 1 ≤ ask they never trade, so they cannot hurt me.
- **Noise traders** value it at 1 + N(0, 2.8). On each side my expected profit is d·P(Z > d/2.8), where d is the distance from 1.
- **Best width:** that profit is largest at d/2.8 ≈ 0.75, so d ≈ 2.1. This gives a bid of about -1.1 and an ask of about 3.1.
- **Position limits:** with only two quotes left, they cannot bind.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

Card 2 is a 1, the lowest card in the deck, so the contract is certain to settle at **1**.

- **Informed traders:** they value the contract at exactly 1. Any bid below 1 and ask above 1 means they won't trade.
- **Noise traders:** their valuation is 1 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.8. For each side, I pick the spread x that maximises x · P(noise > x). That optimum is about 0.75 × 2.8 ≈ 2.1.
- **Quote:** this gives a bid of 1 − 2.1 = −1.1 and an ask of 1 + 2.1 = 3.1.
- **Position check:** I'm long 1, so a fill on either side stays within the ±3 limit.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}
